problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-6y=18x+3.
$$
worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-6y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -6 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)(\lambda -3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =-2$ or $\lambda =3,$ and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-2x}+B{e}^{3x}.
$$

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $1.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular integral is also a polynomial of degree $1,$ i.e.

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha x+\beta 
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha ,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=0
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
0-\alpha -6(\alpha x+\beta )=18x+3
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
-6\alpha x+(-\alpha -6\beta )=18x+3.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}-6\alpha =18\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ -\alpha -6\beta =3\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-3,\beta =0.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-3x.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-2x}+B{e}^{3x}-3x.
$$
